interactions.label: In post-polio residual paralysis, deformity arises from the unopposed pull of mu

params.question: In post-polio residual paralysis, deformity arises from the unopposed pull of muscles that still have nerve supply. Why is tendon transfer the appropriate surgical strategy, rather than tendon lengthening?

answers.text: Tendon lengthening would further weaken an already spastic muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In PPRP, muscles are flaccid, not spastic. Spasticity is an upper motor neurone feature seen in cerebral palsy, where tendon lengthening is the appropriate approach.

answers.text: The upper motor neurone pathway is intact and only needs mechanical redirection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In PPRP, the lower motor neurone (anterior horn cell) is destroyed. The upper motor neurone pathway is affected in cerebral palsy, not in polio.

answers.text: The paralysed muscle has lost its nerve supply entirely and needs a functioning muscle to replace it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The anterior horn cell is destroyed and the muscle is permanently denervated. Tendon transfer borrows a functioning muscle to take over the lost movement.

answers.text: The muscles are hypertonic and shortened, requiring power redistribution rather than release

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PPRP muscles are hypotonic and wasted, not hypertonic. Hypertonia with shortened muscles is the hallmark of cerebral palsy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the LMN-versus-UMN contrast. In PPRP the muscle has lost its nerve supply entirely, so the surgical goal is to borrow a functioning muscle (transfer), not release a tight one (lengthening).
Well done. The key insight is that a denervated muscle cannot be lengthened into usefulness — it needs a working replacement via tendon transfer.

interactions.label: In cerebral palsy, because the brain lesion is non-progressive, the musculoskele

params.question: In cerebral palsy, because the brain lesion is non-progressive, the musculoskeletal deformities also remain stable throughout childhood.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is a common misconception. The brain lesion itself does not worsen, but spastic muscles cause progressive contractures and bony deformities as the child grows. Without intervention, function often deteriorates significantly despite the static neurology.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Although the brain lesion in cerebral palsy is static, the musculoskeletal consequences — contractures, skeletal deformity, gait deterioration — are dynamic and often worsen as the child grows without proactive management.

interactions.label: A 12-year-old with post-polio residual paralysis has a fixed equinovarus deformi

params.question: A 12-year-old with post-polio residual paralysis has a fixed equinovarus deformity and a paralysed tibialis anterior. The surgeon plans a tibialis posterior transfer to restore dorsiflexion. What must be done before the tendon transfer can proceed?

answers.text: Begin intensive hydrotherapy to strengthen the tibialis posterior to grade 5

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grade 4 power is sufficient for a tendon transfer donor. The critical prerequisite is correcting the fixed deformity first — a transfer onto a stiff, misaligned joint will fail regardless of donor muscle strength.

answers.text: Delay surgery until the convalescent stage of neurological recovery is complete

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At age 12, this patient is well past the convalescent stage, which ends by two years after the illness. The residual stage is when corrective and reconstructive surgery is appropriately planned.

answers.text: Correct the fixed equinovarus deformity to achieve a plantigrade foot

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The management hierarchy requires deformity correction before reconstruction. A tendon transfer onto an uncorrected rigid deformity stretches under abnormal tension and the joint cannot move through the required range.

answers.text: Fit a knee-ankle-foot orthosis to permanently stabilise the limb and bypass the deformity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An orthosis supports function but does not address the fixed bony and soft-tissue deformity. The contracture must be surgically corrected before any tendon transfer to ensure the joint can move through its full arc.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the strict management hierarchy: corrective procedures to address fixed deformity must precede any reconstructive tendon transfer. Without a plantigrade, mobile joint, the transferred tendon cannot function effectively.
Exactly right. The hierarchy — conservative, then corrective, then reconstructive — exists because transferring a tendon onto an uncorrected deformity guarantees mechanical failure.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy has dynamic equinus that limit

params.question: A 6-year-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy has dynamic equinus that limits walking. Physiotherapy alone has not controlled the calf spasticity. Which intervention provides a temporary reduction in spasticity for three to six months while physiotherapy consolidates the gain?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Selective dorsal rhizotomy permanently reduces spasticity by cutting selected sensory nerve rootlets. It is reserved for carefully selected children and sits at the permanent end of the treatment spectrum, not the temporary end.

answers.text: Botulinum toxin injection into the calf muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Botulinum toxin temporarily blocks nerve signals to overactive muscles, reducing spasticity for three to six months. This window allows intensive physiotherapy to consolidate range-of-motion gains.

Intrathecal baclofen provides continuous spasticity reduction via a surgically implanted pump. It is used for more severe or widespread spasticity and is further along the escalation spectrum than what this scenario requires.
An AFO holds the ankle in a functional position and stretches the calf, but it does not reduce spasticity itself. It complements spasticity management but is not a spasticity-reducing intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the spasticity management spectrum: botulinum toxin (temporary, 3–6 months) → oral or intrathecal baclofen (continuous) → selective dorsal rhizotomy (permanent). This scenario calls for a temporary intervention at the mildest end.
Well done. Botulinum toxin sits at the temporary end of the spasticity spectrum, providing a therapeutic window for physiotherapy before considering more permanent options.

interactions.label: A surgeon transfers a functioning tendon in a patient with post-polio residual p

params.question: A surgeon transfers a functioning tendon in a patient with post-polio residual paralysis, but the receiving joint has a fixed contracture that was not corrected beforehand. Which analysis best explains why this transfer is likely to fail?

answers.text: The anterior horn cells will not reinnervate the transferred muscle across a deformed joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tendon transfer does not depend on reinnervation of the paralysed muscle. The transferred tendon already has its own intact nerve supply from a different anterior horn cell; the failure mechanism is purely mechanical.

answers.text: Spastic co-contraction of the antagonist will overpower the transferred tendon at the new insertion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spastic co-contraction is a feature of upper motor neurone lesions such as cerebral palsy. In post-polio paralysis, tone is flaccid and there is no spasticity to oppose the transfer.

answers.text: Intact sensation at the transfer site causes pain that inhibits active contraction of the donor muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sensation is completely normal in PPRP because poliovirus selectively attacks motor neurones. Normal sensation does not inhibit tendon transfer function — it actually aids proprioceptive retraining.

answers.text: The tendon stretches under abnormal tension and the joint cannot move through the range the tendon requires

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A fixed deformity places the transferred tendon at a mechanical disadvantage — it stretches over a misaligned joint and cannot generate useful movement through the required arc of motion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The failure is mechanical, not neurological. A tendon transferred onto an uncorrected joint stretches under abnormal tension and cannot move through the range it needs. This is why the hierarchy demands corrective surgery before any reconstructive transfer.
Exactly. The management hierarchy requires deformity correction before reconstruction because a mechanically disadvantaged tendon — stretched over a stiff, misaligned joint — cannot restore function.
